processing: Ripe pu-erh from large-leaf arbor tea, fermented in a controlled pile and pressed into cakes. Batches can include some pre-aged material, so the blend varies.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking: it is a factory recipe blended from stored maocha.
appearance_dry: A brown cake of ripe large-leaf tea, typical of factory ripe pu-erh.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, as usual for ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft dark brown leaf, as usual for ripe pu-erh.
taste_profile: Little independent tasting is on record; expect the usual ripe pu-erh profile of earth, wood and dark sweetness, with some piling aroma when young.

brewing.notes: Standard ripe handling: rinse once, use near-boiling water and lengthen steeps gradually.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year under the Lao Tong Zhi label, with recent retail listings for 2022 and 2025 pressings. A listing notes that the pressing year does not rule out some older material in the blend. Like other ripe recipes it can be drunk young, and a year or more of rest usually softens the pile aroma.
description:
9978 is a numbered ripe recipe from Haiwan, the Yunnan tea company best known for its Lao Tong Zhi label. Numbers like this are how pu-erh factories mark a repeatable blend, so what you are buying is a house recipe rather than a place or a season.

The tea is large-leaf arbor material fermented in a controlled pile and then pressed. Retail listings give its origin around Anning, near Kunming, and one says some batches use pre-aged tea, which means two years of 9978 need not taste the same.

Tasting records are thin. As with other factory ripe cakes, look for earth, wood and a dark sweetness, and brew it with very hot water after a quick rinse.

Check the label, the pressing year and the batch details when buying, and compare weights too: at least one retail pressing is a small 100 g cake, so the price of a cake says little until you work it out per gram.
history: Little is documented about when the 9978 recipe was created or who designed it. Retailers treat it as a classic Lao Tong Zhi recipe, and Haiwan is described as a largely export-minded maker of the Jia Jia and Lao Tong Zhi brands.
